GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrexia of U:
Fever is a measured pyrexia; the task is to separate the septic patient needing immediate treatment from an undifferentiated or prolonged fever needing a staged search. First exclude the emergencies: sepsis (fever with organ dysfunction → the Sepsis 6) (see sepsis), meningococcal disease (fever + a non-blanching rash) (see meningococcal disease) and neutropenic sepsis in the recently chemotherapy-treated patient (see neutropenic sepsis). When a fever >38.3°C persists for >3 weeks and is undiagnosed after initial workup, it is a pyrexia of unknown origin (see pyrexia of unknown origin), whose causes are infection, malignancy, connective-tissue disease and miscellaneous. Foreground lymphoma / leukaemia (see lymphoma), TB (see tuberculosis), infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis) and the returning traveller (see fever in the returning traveller, returning traveller). The rule: treat sepsis now, then investigate systematically.
🚨Treat sepsis before you chase the source. Fever with any organ dysfunction, hypotension or a raised lactate is sepsis — take blood cultures and lactate, give oxygen, IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics (the Sepsis 6) within the hour (see sepsis). A non-blanching purpuric rash with fever is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise — give antibiotics immediately (see meningococcal disease). A fever in a patient within weeks of chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis — a medical emergency treated within one hour (see neutropenic sepsis). Beware the frail elderly, who may be septic without a fever.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss:
Unintentional weight loss — clinically significant at >5% of body weight over 6–12 months — demands a cause be found before it is blamed on age or mood. The red-flag cluster is weight loss with anorexia, night sweats or a mass, which points to malignancy (GI — colorectal, gastric, pancreatic; lung; haematological) (see colorectal cancer, lymphoma) and to chronic infection such as TB or HIV (see tuberculosis, HIV). Metabolic causes are common: hyperthyroidism (weight loss despite a good appetite) (see hyperthyroidism), new diabetes (polyuria + polydipsia) (see type 1 diabetes) and malabsorption (coeliac, pancreatic insufficiency) (see coeliac disease). Do not forget the psychosocial — depression, eating disorders and poverty (see depressive disorders, eating disorders). Quantify the loss, screen broadly and investigate the red flags urgently, and beware cachexia (see cachexia).
🚨Unexplained weight loss is a cancer red flag. Weight loss with anorexia, night sweats, a mass or lymphadenopathy mandates urgent investigation for malignancy (see colorectal cancer, lymphoma). Weight loss with fever and night sweats raises TB and HIV (see tuberculosis, HIV). Rapid weight loss with polyuria, polydipsia and ketosis is new type 1 diabetes that can progress to DKA (see type 1 diabetes). Never attribute weight loss to depression or age until organic disease is excluded — the mistake costs late diagnoses.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tiredness:
Fatigue is one of the commonest presentations; most is benign, but a minority hides serious organic disease. Screen first for the red-flag cluster — fatigue with weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy or bleeding points to malignancy / haematological disease (see lymphoma, leukaemia). The common treatable organic causes are anaemia (see anaemia), hypothyroidism (see hypothyroidism), diabetes (see type 2 diabetes), chronic kidney / liver / heart disease, coeliac disease and sleep apnoea (see snoring & apnoeas). The commonest single cause is psychological — depression and anxiety (see depressive disorders). Consider Addison’s in fatigue with postural dizziness and pigmentation (see Addison’s disease), and medications. Chronic fatigue syndrome is a positive diagnosis made only after exclusion (see chronic fatigue syndrome).
🚨Do not miss the sinister cause of fatigue. Fatigue with weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, bone pain or easy bruising / bleeding points to lymphoma, leukaemia or myeloma and needs urgent bloods and a film (see leukaemia, myeloma). Fatigue with breathlessness and pallor may be severe anaemia (see anaemia). Fatigue with postural collapse, pigmentation, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia may be an Addisonian crisis (see Addison’s disease). Never diagnose chronic fatigue syndrome without first excluding organic disease.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Malaise:
Lethargy and malaise are a vague sense of being unwell or run down — often the earliest, non-specific herald of significant illness, especially in the elderly. In the frail, older or immunosuppressed patient, malaise may be the only sign of sepsis or a metabolic emergency — check observations, glucose, U&E and calcium early (see sepsis). Organic causes overlap with fatigue: anaemia (see anaemia), thyroid disease (see hypothyroidism), diabetes, renal / hepatic failure (see chronic kidney disease), occult infection (EBV, HIV, hepatitis) (see viral infections, HIV), malignancy and adrenal insufficiency (see Addison’s disease). Psychological and iatrogenic causes — depression and medications — are common (see depressive disorders, polypharmacy). Never dismiss malaise in the vulnerable.
🚨Malaise in the vulnerable is an emergency until proven otherwise. In the frail, older or immunosuppressed, malaise with a fever, tachycardia or new confusion may be the only sign of sepsis — septic-screen with a low threshold (see sepsis). Malaise can be the face of a metabolic emergency — DKA, hypercalcaemia, hyponatraemia, an Addisonian crisis or uraemia — so check glucose, U&E and calcium early (see Addison’s disease, hypercalcaemia). Do not label a run-down elderly patient as “just tired” without observations and basic bloods.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised Lymphade:
Generalised lymphadenopathy is enlarged nodes in two or more non-contiguous regions — distinct from a single or regional node (see localised lymphadenopathy). The must-not-miss is haematological malignancy — lymphoma (painless rubbery nodes + B symptoms) (see lymphoma) and leukaemia (nodes + cytopenias / bruising) (see leukaemia) — both needing a tissue diagnosis. The commonest cause is infective: EBV / CMV (young, sore throat, splenomegaly), HIV seroconversion, TB and toxoplasmosis (see viral infections, HIV, tuberculosis). GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats:
True night sweats are drenching sweats that soak nightclothes and bedding — a classic B symptom that must be taken seriously when persistent. The must-not-miss cluster is night sweats with weight loss and fever, pointing to lymphoma / leukaemia (see lymphoma, leukaemia), TB (see tuberculosis) and infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis). Consider HIV and deep infection (see HIV), and endocrine causes such as hyperthyroidism and phaeochromocytoma (see hyperthyroidism). The commonest benign causes are menopause (vasomotor flushes) (see menopausal symptoms), nocturnal hypoglycaemia in treated diabetes (see type 1 diabetes), medications (SSRIs, opioids) (see polypharmacy), GORD and anxiety. Distinguish these from the drenching, B-symptom pattern that demands a search for malignancy and infection.
🚨Drenching night sweats with weight loss are a red flag. Persistent night sweats soaking the bedding, with weight loss and fever, point to lymphoma or leukaemia and mandate a FBC, film, LDH and imaging (see lymphoma). Night sweats with a chronic cough and haemoptysis suggest TB (see tuberculosis); with a new murmur and fever, infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis). Do not reassure a patient with true drenching sweats and systemic symptoms as “menopause” or “stress” before excluding malignancy and infection.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appetite:
Loss of appetite (anorexia) is a reduced desire to eat — important as an early, non-specific marker of serious organic disease, and distinct from anorexia nervosa. The must-not-miss causes are malignancy (the anorexia–cachexia syndrome) (see colorectal cancer, lymphoma, cachexia) and occult sepsis in the frail elderly (see sepsis). GI and metabolic causes are common: peptic / gastric disease and dysphagia (see dyspepsia), hepatic / renal failure (see chronic kidney disease), hypercalcaemia (see hypercalcaemia), hyponatraemia, Addison’s and hypothyroidism. Do not forget the psychiatric and iatrogenic — depression (a leading cause) (see depressive disorders), eating disorders in the young (see eating disorders), dementia / frailty, and appetite-suppressing drugs (see polypharmacy). Quantify intake and weight, and support nutrition (see malnutrition).
🚨New anorexia can be the first sign of cancer or sepsis. Loss of appetite with weight loss and cachexia warrants a search for malignancy (see colorectal cancer). In a frail elderly patient, anorexia may be the only new symptom of occult sepsis or a metabolic derangement — check observations, glucose, U&E and calcium (see sepsis, hypercalcaemia). In the young, a fear of weight gain and distorted body image points to an eating disorder needing specialist assessment and monitoring for refeeding risk (see eating disorders). Weigh the patient and quantify intake — do not accept “poor appetite” without a cause.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls:
Falls in older adults are usually multifactorial; the job is to separate a mechanical trip from a fall that signals cardiac, neurological or acute medical disease (see falls in the elderly). A fall with true loss of consciousness suggests cardiac syncope — arrhythmia, aortic stenosis or PE (see syncope, valvular heart disease). Always look hard for injury (head injury on anticoagulants, a neck-of-femur fracture) (see NOF fracture) and for a fall as the presentation of sepsis, MI or stroke (see sepsis). The common contributors are postural hypotension and culprit medications (see polypharmacy), gait / balance and neurological disorders, visual impairment, arthritis, deconditioning and environmental hazards. Assess every domain and treat reversible factors (see falls assessment, frailty).
🚨A fall can be syncope, injury or acute illness in disguise. A fall with loss of consciousness, no warning or on exertion may be cardiac syncope — arrhythmia or aortic stenosis — and needs a 12-lead ECG (see syncope, valvular heart disease). A head strike on anticoagulants risks intracranial haemorrhage (see reduced consciousness); a painful, shortened and externally rotated leg is a neck-of-femur fracture (see NOF fracture). A fall with new confusion and fever may be the presentation of sepsis (see sepsis). Examine for injury and screen for an acute medical cause in every faller.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Frailty & Functional:
Frailty is a state of reduced physiological reserve; the key rule is that “acopia” is never a diagnosis — always find the cause of decline. An acute or subacute decline (“off legs”) is acute illness until proven otherwise — sepsis, MI, stroke, AKI, delirium and medication toxicity all present this way (see off legs, sepsis, delirium). Grade frailty with the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale (see frailty) and recognise the frailty syndromes — falls, immobility, incontinence and delirium. Address the contributors: polypharmacy (see polypharmacy), malnutrition / sarcopenia (see malnutrition), cognitive impairment (see dementia), depression (see depressive disorders) and social factors. The framework is the Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (see comprehensive geriatric assessment) — multidisciplinary, aiming to restore function.
🚨“Off legs” is acute illness until proven otherwise. A sudden or subacute functional decline in an older person is a presentation of sepsis, MI, stroke, AKI, delirium or drug toxicity — not simply “social” (see off legs, sepsis). Delirium — acute, fluctuating inattention — is common, dangerous and reversible; screen with the 4AT and find the cause (see delirium). Never label a patient as “acopia” or “poor historian” and never discharge a decline without excluding acute medical illness and doing a proper functional and cognitive assessment.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained Collapse:
An unexplained collapse is a transient loss of consciousness with spontaneous recovery; the first task is to separate cardiac syncope from neurological and reflex causes (see transient loss of consciousness, syncope). Cardiac syncope kills — arrhythmia, aortic stenosis, HOCM and PE cause sudden, exertional or unheralded collapse, and a 12-lead ECG is mandatory in every patient (see valvular heart disease, pulmonary embolism). The commonest causes are reflex (vasovagal) and orthostatic hypotension (see syncope). Distinguish a seizure (tongue-biting, post-ictal confusion) (see seizures) and hypoglycaemia (see type 1 diabetes) from true syncope. Take an eyewitness history, do an ECG and a lying / standing BP, and refer red-flag features urgently.
🚨A 12-lead ECG is mandatory in every collapse. Red-flag features — collapse on exertion, without warning, causing injury, or with a family history of sudden cardiac death or an abnormal ECG — point to cardiac syncope (arrhythmia, aortic stenosis, HOCM) and need urgent cardiology (see syncope, valvular heart disease). Collapse with breathlessness, hypoxia or pleuritic pain may be PE (see pulmonary embolism). Do not attribute a collapse to a “simple faint” without an eyewitness account, an ECG and a lying / standing blood pressure.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Cardiac syncope
  • Sudden collapse, no warning or on exertion, rapid recovery
  • Arrhythmia (brady / tachy), aortic stenosis, HOCM (see syncope, valvular heart disease)
  • A 12-lead ECG is mandatory; red flags → urgent cardiology
🚩Pulmonary embolism / catastrophe
  • Collapse + breathlessness + hypoxia + pleuritic pain → PE (see pulmonary embolism)
  • Also massive GI bleed, ruptured AAA, subarachnoid haemorrhage
  • A haemodynamic or hypoxic collapse is not a simple faint
🟠Vasovagal (reflex) syncope
  • A prodrome (nausea, sweating, tunnel vision) + a trigger (standing, pain, emotion)
  • Rapid, complete recovery — the commonest cause (see syncope)
  • Situational (cough, micturition) syncope is a variant
🟠Orthostatic hypotension
  • Collapse on standing with a fall in blood pressure (see transient loss of consciousness)
  • Drugs, dehydration, autonomic failure
  • Confirm with a lying / standing blood pressure
🩹Seizure
  • Tonic-clonic movements, tongue-biting, incontinence, post-ictal confusion (see seizures)
  • A prolonged recovery distinguishes it from syncope
  • Get a witness account and consider EEG / imaging
🩹Metabolic / mechanical
  • Hypoglycaemia — collapse relieved by sugar (see type 1 diabetes)
  • A mechanical fall without loss of consciousness
  • Check a capillary glucose in every collapse
Cardiac, reflex or neurological? An eyewitness account, a 12-lead ECG and a lying / standing BP resolve most collapses. Exertional, unheralded or injurious collapse, or an abnormal ECG, is cardiac until excluded; a prodrome with a trigger is vasovagal; tongue-biting and post-ictal confusion suggest a seizure.

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised / System:
Generalised oedema is bilateral, dependent, pitting fluid overload; the first split is systemic (bilateral) versus localised (unilateral — DVT, cellulitis, lymphoedema) (see swollen leg). The three great causes are cardiac (heart failure) (see chronic heart failure), renal (nephrotic syndrome, CKD) (see glomerulonephritis) and hepatic (cirrhosis) (see liver cirrhosis) — plus hypoalbuminaemia from malnutrition or protein loss (see malnutrition). Nephrotic oedema is periorbital with frothy urine (see proteinuria, periorbital oedema); hepatic oedema comes with ascites and stigmata (see ascites). Also consider drugs (calcium-channel blockers, NSAIDs, steroids) and venous disease (see polypharmacy). Urgently treat pulmonary oedema, and never mistake a unilateral hot leg for systemic overload.
🚨Two traps in generalised oedema. First, cardiac failure with pulmonary oedema — bilateral pitting oedema with orthopnoea, a raised JVP and lung crepitations — needs urgent treatment (see acute heart failure). Second, never mistake a unilateral hot, swollen, tender leg (a DVT) for systemic oedema — it needs a Doppler and anticoagulation, not diuretics (see swollen leg, DVT / PE). And sudden facial and tongue swelling is angioedema / anaphylaxis, not dependent oedema, and can obstruct the airway (see anaphylaxis). Bilateral, dependent and pitting is systemic; unilateral or acute facial is not.

🚩Cardiac failure / pulmonary oedema
  • Bilateral pitting oedema + orthopnoea + raised JVP + lung crepitations
  • Acute pulmonary oedema needs urgent treatment (see acute heart failure)

🟠Nephrotic syndrome (renal)
  • Periorbital oedema + frothy urine + hypoalbuminaemia (see proteinuria)
  • Heavy proteinuria on urinalysis → nephrotic syndrome (see glomerulonephritis)
  • CKD also causes fluid retention (see periorbital oedema)
🟠Hepatic (cirrhosis)
  • Oedema + ascites + jaundice + spider naevi (see ascites)
  • Low albumin and portal hypertension (see liver cirrhosis)
  • Look for stigmata of chronic liver disease
🩹Hypoalbuminaemia / malnutrition
  • Low albumin from poor intake or protein loss (see malnutrition)
  • Protein-losing enteropathy and severe illness
  • Generalised oedema with a low serum albumin
🩹Drug-induced / venous
  • Calcium-channel blockers (amlodipine), NSAIDs, steroids (see polypharmacy)
  • Chronic venous insufficiency — bilateral dependent oedema
  • Myxoedema (hypothyroidism) — non-pitting

GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration & Fluid:
Dehydration and fluid depletion are a deficit of body water ± sodium; assess severity and find the cause. Grade the deficit clinically — observations, mucous membranes, capillary refill, skin turgor, urine output and urea. The emergency is hypovolaemic shock (tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, a raised lactate) needing immediate fluid resuscitation (see shock, shock assessment). Behind severe depletion, think DKA / HHS (see type 1 diabetes), a GI catastrophe and sepsis (see sepsis). The causes are losses — GI (vomiting, diarrhoea, high-output stoma) (see diarrhoea), renal (diuretics, osmotic diuresis, diabetes insipidus, Addison’s) (see diabetes insipidus, Addison’s disease) and skin — and reduced intake / redistribution (frail elderly, third-spacing in pancreatitis) (see frailty, acute pancreatitis). Resuscitate, then replace the deficit and ongoing losses (see acute kidney injury).
🚨Hypovolaemic shock needs immediate fluid resuscitation. Tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria and a raised lactate signal shock — give a fluid challenge and reassess, and identify the source of loss (see shock). Behind severe depletion, think DKA / HHS (thirst, ketones, high glucose) (see type 1 diabetes), a GI catastrophe (bleeding, obstruction) and sepsis with distributive loss (see sepsis). In the frail elderly, dehydration presents as confusion, a raised urea and pre-renal AKI (see acute kidney injury). Match the fluid to the deficit and the electrolytes — do not under-resuscitate a shocked patient.

🚩Hypovolaemic shock
  • Tachycardia + hypotension + oliguria + raised lactate + cool peripheries
  • Immediate fluid resuscitation and reassessment (see shock, shock assessment)
  • Find and control the source of loss
🚩DKA / HHS / severe sepsis
  • DKA / HHS — thirst, polyuria, ketones, high glucose, huge fluid deficit (see type 1 diabetes)
  • Septic (distributive) hypovolaemia — fever + vasodilatation (see sepsis)
  • Check glucose, ketones and a venous gas
🟠GI losses
  • Vomiting, diarrhoea, a high-output stoma or fistula (see diarrhoea)
  • Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, thirst
  • Replace water and electrolytes guided by U&E
🟠Reduced intake (elderly / frail)
  • Poor oral intake, dysphagia or immobility in the frail (see frailty)
  • Presents as confusion, a raised urea and pre-renal AKI
  • Assess swallow and support hydration
🩹Renal / drug losses
  • Diuretics and osmotic diuresis (glycosuria) (see polypharmacy)
  • Diabetes insipidus — polyuria with dilute urine (see diabetes insipidus)
  • Addison’s — salt-wasting, hyponatraemia (see Addison’s disease)
🩹Third-spacing / redistribution
  • Pancreatitis, bowel obstruction and sepsis sequester fluid (see acute pancreatitis)
  • Intravascular depletion despite total-body fluid
  • Burns and severe hypoalbuminaemia also third-space
Resuscitate first, then diagnose the loss. Treat hypovolaemic shock with a fluid challenge and reassess; check glucose, ketones and a gas. Then classify the cause — GI, renal, reduced intake or redistribution — and replace the deficit and ongoing losses with the right fluid.
